statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 10 are written on a board. A move is to erase two numbers and write either their sum or the larger minus the smaller (which is 0 if they are equal). After nine moves one number remains. How many different values could it have?

choices.misconception: I thought the last number is fixed, as it would be if only sums were allowed, so only one value is possible.
I found that the possible values are the odd numbers from 1 to 55 but counted them as (55 - 1)/2 = 27, forgetting to add one.
I thought every value from 1 to 55 is possible, missing that the parity of the total never changes.
I thought every value from 0 to 55 is possible, ignoring parity altogether.

hints: What happens to the parity of the total on the board after one move?

Replacing a and b by a + b or by their difference keeps the total of all numbers on the board odd or even as before. That limits the last number; then check which allowed values can really be reached.
The starting total is 55, which is odd, and no move ever increases the total.

solutions.reliable: The sum a + b and the difference of a and b always have the same parity, so each move keeps the parity of the total. The total starts at 55, which is odd, so the last number is odd; it is also at most 55, since no move increases the total. That leaves the 28 odd numbers 1, 3, ..., 55. All of them occur: for an odd v below 55, pick some of the numbers adding up to s = (55 - v)/2 (every total from 1 to 27 can be made from different numbers between 1 and 10), add them into a single number s, add the rest into 55 - s, and finish with (55 - s) - s = v. Using sums alone gives 55. So exactly 28 values are possible. The transferable idea: an invariant shows what is impossible and a construction shows everything else is possible; an exact count needs both.

whyOnTest: The parity invariant halves the possibilities, and the 5-point step is showing that every surviving odd value can actually be reached.
